prompt: Could you write a captivating short story beginning with the sentence: The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.
answer:
The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

Then, on the evening before its demolition, Rose heard someone inside whistling her husband’s song.

She stopped beneath the chestnut tree.

It was a foolish little tune. Arthur had invented it because he couldn’t whistle anything anybody else had written. Three rising notes, two falling, then a breathless scramble that always made her laugh.

Arthur had been dead for sixty-two years.

Rose put her shopping bag on the pavement.

“Do that again,” she said.

From inside the house came three rising notes.

***

The front door opened when she touched it.

She had expected rotting floorboards, perhaps teenagers with a radio. Instead, she found a railway waiting room.

Rain streaked the tall windows. A coal fire burned in the grate. Above a ticket office, a clock showed seventeen minutes past eight.

A young woman slept beneath a newspaper dated 1931. A sailor sat with his hands folded over a parcel. Beside the fire stood a man in a brown suit, trying to whistle while he examined a broken watch.

Rose knew the suit. She had let out its cuffs herself.

“Arthur.”

He looked up.

For a moment he wore the polite, uncertain smile he reserved for strangers. Then his eyes moved across her face.

“Rose?”

She had imagined this reunion so often that she had worn out all the things she might say.

What came out was, “Your train never arrived.”

“I know. We stopped somewhere.” He glanced at the clock. “There’s been a delay.”

“The bridge collapsed.”

His hand closed around the watch.

“They searched for weeks,” she said. “They found your suitcase.”

Around them, the other passengers had become very still.

Arthur looked at her white hair, her walking stick, the wedding ring buried in the soft folds of her finger.

“How long?”

She told him.

He sat down.

Rose remained standing. Her knees hurt. It seemed suddenly outrageous that her knees should hurt while Arthur still had the face she remembered pressing against a train window.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She almost laughed.

“I was so angry with you.”

“I tried to get home.”

“I know.”

“No.” He looked towards the dark windows. “I think I’ve been trying for a very long time.”

Behind the ticket-office grille, someone cleared his throat.

An elderly porter stood there now.

“Is he yours, madam?”

Rose looked back at Arthur.

“We were married,” she said.

The porter took a ledger from a shelf. Every page was crowded with names.

“Then you can take him.”

“What is this place?”

“Where they wait when the journey breaks.”

“And all these people?”

The sailor lowered his eyes to his parcel.

“Sometimes,” said the porter, “it takes a while for someone to find the door.”

Rose turned towards the entrance. Through its glass she could see her shopping bag beneath the chestnut tree.

“If he comes with me?”

“He comes with you.”

She wanted a warning, a condition, something that would make this terrible kindness comprehensible.

The porter merely held out Arthur’s hat.

***

At the threshold, Arthur stopped.

“You had a life?”

“Yes.”

“Was it good?”

She thought of the school where she had taught for thirty years. Her garden. Her friends. Daniel, whom she had married at forty and buried at seventy-three.

“Much of it.”

“Good,” Arthur said, though he needed a moment before he could say it.

Then he looked down at her hand.

“The baby?”

Rose’s grip tightened around her stick.

“A boy.”

Arthur shut his eyes.

“He’s got your ears,” she said.

“Poor little fellow.”

“He’s retired.”

That undid him.

She waited while he cried. Then she took his hand, and they stepped outside.

***

Her son arrived twenty minutes after she telephoned.

He came through the kitchen door carrying his usual bag of tools, because Rose had said there was something at the house he needed to see.

Arthur stood up.

For a long moment, neither man moved.

Her son set the tools down carefully.

“All right,” he said, in a voice Rose hadn’t heard since he was small.

Arthur reached into his coat.

“I bought you something. At the station. I didn’t know whether you’d be a boy or a girl, but—”

He held out a little wooden engine, its red paint bright beneath the kitchen light.

His son took it. Turned it over. Ran one broad thumb along its tiny wheels.

“I used to wish for one of these,” he said.

Then he stepped forward, and Arthur put his arms around his child.
